Population levels for non-Crows in the area should tend to be somewhat proportionate to their employment levels. The analysis shows that for non-Crows the difference in populations between Scenario 2 and Scenario 1 would be only about 311 people. Thus, an increase of 3.8 percent would be the net effect of higher level development on total employment in the impact area.
With other significant Crow coal development taking place (AF-2) the total employment rises sharply. If the Crow labor force participation rate does not increase, the bulk of the increased employment will be non-Crow. As shown by Figure III-12 if the Crow participation rate remains constant, Crow employment raises approximately in proportion to their population, leaving an unmet labor demand which would be filled by non-Crows.
This set of circumstances would approximately double non-Crow employment between 1975 and 2000 by increasing employment from 2363 to 4628. Relatively constant levels would occur after 1990 for both scenarios.
Under Scenario 2, over twice as many non-Crows (4628 vs 2363) would be employed in the year 2000 than in 1970. Crow employment although more than doubling (from 729 to 1872), would fall far short of realizing maximum potential employment.
